description: Universal Display Corporation engages in the research, development, and commercialization of organic light emitting diode (OLED) technologies and materials for use in display and solid-state lighting
description_full: Universal Display Corporation engages in the research, development, and commercialization of organic light emitting diode (OLED) technologies and materials for use in display and solid-state lighting applications. It offers phosphorescent organic light-emitting diode (PHOLED) technologies and materials for displays and lighting products under the UniversalPHOLED brand. The company also offers FOLED that are flexible OLEDs for the fabrication of OLEDs on flexible substrates; and OVJP, an organic vapor jet printing technology. In addition, it provides technology development and support services, including third-party collaboration and support to third parties for the commercialization of their OLED products; and contract research services in the areas of chemical synthesis research, development, and commercialization for non-OLED applications, as well as engages in the intellectual property and technology licensing activities. The company has operations in South Korea, China, Japan, the United States, and internationally. Universal Display Corporation was incorporated in 1985 and is headquartered in Ewing, New Jersey.

culture_narrative: Employs approximately 469 people. Revenue per employee of $1.4M ranks in the top quartile among Technology peers, improving at 17%/yr — growing workforce leverage. Each employee generates $329K of free cash flow annually. Stock-based compensation of $60K per employee reflects an ownership culture. CEO compensation is 2× revenue per employee (modest relative to workforce productivity). Governance score flags elevated compensation governance risk (9/10).
financial_summary: Universal Display Corporation is a mid-cap technology business with a $4.0B market cap on $651M of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at +2% over the past three years and +13% annually across the full decade, which puts it in mature, slow-growth territory.
Returns on capital run at 22% against a 11% cost of capital — a 11-point spread that is the clearest signature of an economic moat. Gross margins of 79% confirm genuine pricing power.

The business throws off $154M in free cash flow — roughly 24 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, with adequate 0.87× cash conversion.
On the balance sheet, the balance sheet carries net cash, which is the gold standard: the business never has to make desperate decisions in a bad year.

Shareholder yield of 2.9% reflects a genuine commitment to returning capital rather than empire-building, and insiders hold 8.5% of the shares, and within its sector the business captures 1.6× its fair share of profits, a structural advantage visible in the numbers.

sect: Its 38% operating margin runs 31pp above the Technology median (7%), a real cost or pricing edge over peers.
It captures 1.63x its revenue share in sector profits, taking a disproportionate slice of the profit pool.
Over five years it has been losing share of the sector profit pool (-6.2% a year).
The sector is fragmented and competitive (HHI 0.03 across 530 companies in the universe; the top four hold 29% of revenue), so pricing power is hard to come by.
mkt: The shares are in a steep downtrend, down 40% over the past year excluding the latest month.
The price sits mid-way through its 52-week range, 34% below the high.
With annualised volatility of 43% and a beta of 1.22, it amplifies market moves, though its beta has shifted (1y 0.54 vs 5y 1.32), so read it loosely.
About $58.0M trades a day, enough to build a position.
In past sell-offs it fell 51% in the 2020 crash, 48% in the 2022 bear market and 76% in 2008.
val: The stock trades 23% below its DCF fair value of $114, a meaningful margin of safety.
The fair-value models disagree (dispersion 43%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $71.38 to $190 (P10-P90), so treat the estimate as noisy.
On multiples it looks cheap against Technology peers: P/E 17.9 vs 26.7 (sector median).
Against its own history it is cheap: the EBIT multiple sits 56% below its 10-year median.
Earnings yields are thin: an FCF yield of 3.9% (below the risk-free rate) and an EBIT/EV of 7.1% (vs the 8% bar).
The 9 covering analysts target $115 on average, 30% above the price.
prof: ROIC of 22% clears the cost of capital of 10.8% by 11pp, the mark of a value creator; returns have swung a lot from year to year (CV 0.61).
It runs a 79% gross margin and converts 24% of revenue into free cash flow, or 19% after stock compensation.
ROE of 14% comes mostly from margins and asset turnover rather than leverage (1.1x equity multiplier).
It spends 22.5% of revenue on R&D and 4.3% on stock compensation (above the 2% gate).
hlth: The balance sheet carries net cash of $602.4M (15% of market cap).
No distress or manipulation flags (Altman Z 13.9, in the safe zone).
growth: Revenue has compounded at 1.8% over 3 years, 8.7% over 5 years and 13.0% over 10 years, so growth is decelerating, and it has been lumpy (year-to-year swings of 30%).
At current returns, reinvesting 100% of profits supports about 22.1% a year of fundamental growth, enough to sustain growth.
Free cash flow has compounded 5.0% a year over five years.
Capex runs 2.0x depreciation (8.7% of sales), so it is building capacity for future growth.
own: Insiders own 8.5%, meaningful skin in the game, and reported institutional holdings exceed 100% of shares (a sign of heavy share lending).
Insider trading is two-way: 7 purchases and 2 sales over the past year, net $1.0M bought.
It returns 2.9% a year to shareholders (0.8% in buybacks and 2.3% in dividends).
The share count has shrunk 1.0% a year over five years, steadily raising each holder's stake.
Short interest is elevated at 10.1% of the float, 6.1 days to cover.
people: With about 469 employees, each generates about $1.4M of revenue, 3.7x the Technology median, and productivity has risen 17.1% a year.
That works out to $329K of free cash flow per employee.
CEO pay is $2.4M (2x revenue per employee), and compensation governance scores poorly (9/10, lower is better).
